name: disintegration
title: Disintegration
question:
Does the paper's §Disintegration level-shift (Fig 6) hold spatially -- a coherent CPM cell that loses structural
viability when a diffusing field of acetate (the SAME metabolic byproduct that is waste-and-food
in `cell-cell-coupling`, here toxic at high local concentration) crosses its viability
bound, its domain resorbing while its shed material becomes scattering physical particles -- composed from independent frameworks
(viva-cpm + spatio-flux particles) through one coupling process (`CpmDisintegration` +
`BrownianMovement`)?
biological_summary:
This is the spatial realization of the paper's §Disintegration pattern
(Fig 6), built on a new coupling process, `CpmDisintegration`, that
owns a single CPM cell (no metabolism/cobra path -- this study is about the viability-collapse
trigger, not nutrient uptake) sitting on a shared spatio-flux `acetate` field. The stressor
species here is literally `acetate` (the process reads it via config `stressor_field: acetate`;
the observable stays named `mean_stressor`) -- the SAME molecule that is the secretor's
metabolic waste and the consumer's sole carbon food in `cell-cell-coupling`. This is
the paper's closing §Disintegration/§Cell–cell coupling claim in action: an environmental
variable acquires its significance relationally, a molecule counting as nutrient, signal, or
toxin through its consequences for viability. The same acetate that keeps a cross-feeding
consumer alive elsewhere becomes, at high local concentration, the toxin that pushes THIS cell
across its viability bound. Each tick the
process reads mean acetate over the cell's own CPM footprint; once that reading crosses
`viability_threshold`, it LATCHES a `released` flag (never un-crosses) and ramps the cell's
target volume toward zero, shedding each tick's vacated footprint pixels as debris particles
into a shared `map[particle]` store that a seeded `SeededBrownianMovement` (a seed-adding subclass of spatio-flux `BrownianMovement`) then scatters.
The CPM-to-particle bridge this depends on -- a process emitting particles via the map `_add`
sentinel that a separate stock movement process then moves -- is no longer an assumption; it is
runtime-verified directly (`tests/test_particle_bridge_spike.py`): three synthetic particles
emitted on one tick are still exactly three particles four ticks later, with at least two of
them having moved.

One tuned regime over `disintegration-spatial`
(`meta_modelers_guide.composites.disintegration-spatial`) demonstrates the full arc:
a single CPM cell centered on a 60x60 shared field grid inside a radial acetate gradient --
low at the grid center where the cell is seeded, rising toward the periphery -- diffusing
under spatio-flux `DiffusionAdvection`. The CPM trajectory -- hold, cross, resorb -- is
fixed-seed deterministic and reproduces exactly run to run (measured over a 20-tick run,
`tests/test_cpm_disintegration.py`, `tests/test_disintegration_regime.py`,
`tests/test_disintegration_viz.py`, verified over repeated runs): the cell holds coherent
(area > 30 pixels) through tick 6 with zero debris, the footprint-local acetate mean (the
observable `mean_stressor`) crosses
`viability_threshold` at `released_tick = 7`, and from there the domain resorbs monotonically
-- area 56 at tick 7 down to area 0 by tick 16 -- while shedding exactly 63 particles into the
debris store (up to 8/tick, capped, until the footprint is exhausted). Every one of those numbers --
`released_tick`, the area trajectory, and the 63-particle shed count -- is reproducible exactly,
because the CPM engine is fixed-seed and the shedding logic is a deterministic function of the
footprint diff. The debris cloud's scatter is now deterministic too: it moves under a seeded
`SeededBrownianMovement` (seed=1, a seed-adding subclass of the stock spatio-flux process, since
the stock one draws from NumPy's global RNG), so the RMS-spread values below are now exactly
reproducible run to run -- `tests/test_disintegration_seed.py` asserts byte-identical debris
positions across two builds -- and the qualitative claim (RMS spread strictly increases after
dissolution completes) is a robust, test-asserted fact on top.
A representative run: RMS spread keeps strictly increasing after dissolution completes (~5.3 at
tick 16 to ~7.6 at tick 24, an 8-tick post-dissolution window) -- genuine scattering, not
particles piling up against a wall or the field boundary. The whole arc -- hold, cross, resorb,
scatter -- is code-verified simulation output from one coupling process plus one seeded
movement process. The trigger timing is simulation-derived (the footprint-local acetate crossing
the viability bound), but the resorption ramp itself is SCRIPTED (resorb_per_tick=6.0), not an
emergent dissolution rate; with the scatter now seeded, the whole arc is reproducible run to run,
magnitude and direction alike.

This is precisely the failure cascade the paper's §Disintegration describes: once viability is
lost, energy production can no longer sustain transport, membranes lose integrity, gradients
collapse, and the system transitions from an actively maintained, far-from-equilibrium state to
one dominated by diffusion, equilibration, and mechanical relaxation. The two phases of the run
read directly as that transition: while the cell holds, an actively maintained CPM domain
resists the rising acetate; once released, the shed material is handed to `BrownianMovement`,
and the scattering debris cloud IS the diffusion-dominated, equilibrating regime -- the
far-from-equilibrium cell relaxing toward equilibrium as literal drifting particles. As the
paper notes, most models do not represent this transition explicitly: agent-based models remove
cells mid-simulation, and whole-cell models assume viability -- so a spatial model that carries
a coherent domain all the way through its own dissolution into diffusing debris is the point.
claim:
Composing one real CPM cell with a real spatio-flux acetate field and a real spatio-flux
particle-movement process through two coupling processes (`CpmDisintegration` for the
viability-collapse trigger and resorption, stock `BrownianMovement` for the debris scatter)
reproduces the paper's §Disintegration level-shift (Fig 6) as spatial dissolution with a SCRIPTED
resorption schedule (resorb_per_tick=6.0): the trigger timing is simulation-derived (the
footprint-local acetate crossing a viability bound), the resorption ramp itself is scripted -- not a
lumped scalar stand-in: over a fixed-seed deterministic 20-tick CPM run, the cell holds coherent
(area > 30) through tick 6, the footprint-local acetate mean crosses viability_threshold at
released_tick = 7, the domain resorbs to area 0 by tick 16, and its 63 shed pixels become a
debris cloud whose RMS spread strictly increases through tick 24 (the trajectory -- hold, cross,
resorb, particle count -- reproduces exactly; the scatter cloud moves under unseeded
`BrownianMovement`, so its exact RMS magnitudes are representative of one run, not
run-to-run-reproducible -- only the strict-increase direction is the robust claim) -- hold,
cross, resorb, scatter, end to end from one coupling process plus one stock movement process,
mirroring a lumped, specification-stage realization's §Disintegration level-shift pattern (Fig 6) at
real spatial, per-pixel resolution.
key_assumptions:
The disintegration mechanism realized here is **resorption + particle-shedding**, not
in-lattice fragmentation. In this `viva-cpm` build the connectivity/"E1" structural-integrity
constraint is a verified no-op (ON and OFF give statistically indistinguishable fragmentation
under fragmenting energetics, and toggling it mid-run changes nothing -- a verified engine
limitation), and `lambda_volume` /
`temperature` are init-only with no runtime setters, so a settled CPM domain cannot be
shattered into scattered pixels in-lattice. The code-verified route taken here is to resorb the
cell (`set_target_volume -> 0`) and convert its shed pixels into particles via a separate,
verified bridge. This is a chosen realization of "the coherent domain dissolves," not
emergent lattice fragmentation -- a real engine limitation.

Debris particles move under spatio-flux `BrownianMovement` -- NumPy diffusion over a bounded
grid -- not rigid-body pymunk physics. The shed particles drift and scatter; they do not
collide with each other, with the dissolving cell, or fall under gravity.

The acetate field's radial gradient (peak 1.5, ring onset at radius 5, saturating at radius
18), `viability_threshold` (0.5), `resorb_per_tick` (6.0), `max_particles_per_tick` (8), and
the diffusion coefficients (acetate D=4.0, debris diffusion_rate=1.0) are toy-real: plausible,
hand-tuned magnitudes chosen to make hold -> cross -> resorb -> scatter all legible within a
20-tick run, not fitted to a named stressor, material, or literature target.

Unlike studies 2-3 in this investigation (`cell-environment-coupling`,
`cell-cell-coupling`), this study's CPM cell has NO metabolism/cobra path at all --
`CpmDisintegration` is deliberately built around the viability-collapse trigger alone, not
nutrient uptake or growth.

The `released` flag LATCHES once the crossing happens and never un-crosses, even once the
footprint empties and its mean-stressor reading would otherwise read 0.0 -- a deliberate design
choice so an emptied, dissolved cell cannot spuriously "recover" viability.

The CPM-to-particle bridge (a process emitting particles via the map `_add` sentinel into a
shared `map[particle]` store, moved by a separate stock `BrownianMovement` process) is no
longer an assumption; it is runtime-verified directly
(`tests/test_particle_bridge_spike.py`) against a synthetic emitter, independently of the
disintegration mechanism itself.
acceptance_criteria: A coherent CPM cell holds its structure while the diffusing acetate field stays below its footprint-local viability bound.
Once the footprint-local acetate crosses that bound, viability latches lost (never un-crosses) and the domain resorbs to full dissolution within the run.
The vacated footprint pixels appear as physical debris particles whose RMS spread strictly increases under Brownian scatter -- particles that drift, rather than vanishing.

The CPM->particle conversion conserves mass -- each shed debris particle is a distinct vacated lattice pixel (no re-vacated pixel shed twice), so the shed count equals the distinct-vacated-pixel count and never exceeds the unique-vacated-pixel total. Shed material, not deleted-then-recreated mass.

units_and_time.time: 1 tick = unspecified physical time (dimensionless model time); the run is 20-24 such ticks.
units_and_time.quantities: field, area, and volume quantities are dimensionless model units -- acetate concentrations, the viability_threshold (0.5), resorb_per_tick (6.0), and diffusion coefficients (acetate D=4.0, debris diffusion_rate=1.0) carry no calibrated physical unit; area and particle counts are lattice-pixel counts, not physical mass.
units_and_time.note: No quantity here is calibrated to a named stressor, material, or literature target.

behavior_tests.name: cell-holds-coherent-before-crossing
behavior_tests.description: Before the acetate crosses viability_threshold, the CPM cell stays coherent (substantial area, released flag unset, no debris) -- the hold phase of the §Disintegration level shift (Fig 6).

pass_if.provenance: prior: a coherent CPM cell holds its structure (substantial footprint area) while the diffusing acetate stays below its footprint-local viability bound -> expect area well above a small floor before the crossing. Observed: area 61-66 through tick 6, released stays False, n_particles == 0 (the 30.0 floor is a post-hoc pin, the >-direction is the a-priori prediction) (tests/test_disintegration_regime.py::test_cell_holds_then_disintegrates_into_scattering_debris, tests/test_cpm_disintegration.py::test_holds_below_threshold)

behavior_tests.name: stressor-crosses-viability-bound
behavior_tests.description: The footprint-local acetate mean crosses viability_threshold and the released flag latches, at a specific, deterministic tick -- the level-shift trigger itself.

measure.expr: obs.released_tick once obs.released first reads True

pass_if.provenance: released latches True at released_tick == 7.0 -- a regression pin set after observing the run, exact only while the fixed-seed CPM engine and gradient are pinned; deterministic across repeated runs of the same composite (tests/test_cpm_disintegration.py::test_releases_and_disintegrates_into_particles, tests/test_disintegration_regime.py)

behavior_tests.name: domain-resorbs-to-zero
behavior_tests.description: Once released, the cell's target volume ramps toward zero and its CPM lattice footprint resorbs to full dissolution well within the run -- the domain genuinely disappearing, not merely shrinking.

pass_if.provenance: prior: once the viability bound is crossed the target volume ramps down and the domain resorbs to full dissolution (area -> 0) within the run. Observed: area falls monotonically from 56 (tick 7) to 0 by tick 16, and stays 0 through tick 20. The == 0.0 endpoint is the a-priori prediction; the exact tick (16) is a pin, exact only while the fixed-seed CPM engine is pinned (tests/test_disintegration_regime.py::test_cell_holds_then_disintegrates_into_scattering_debris, tests/test_cpm_disintegration.py::test_releases_and_disintegrates_into_particles)

behavior_tests.name: shed-material-becomes-debris-particles
behavior_tests.description: The cell's vacated footprint pixels appear as debris particles in the shared map[particle] store as it resorbs, and the CPM->particle conversion conserves mass -- the CPM->particle ledger closes. The shed count (63) exceeds the cell area at the release instant (56 px) not because mass is manufactured but because the footprint DRIFTS and reshapes under Metropolis dynamics while it resorbs, traversing 69 distinct lattice pixels over its released lifetime rather than the 56 held at one instant; each distinct pixel sheds at most one particle (an earlier logic double-shed 6 re-vacated pixels -- 68 particles over 62 distinct pixels -- now fixed with an already-shed-pixel guard). Shed material, not deleted-then-recreated mass.

pass_if.provenance: prior: as the domain resorbs, its vacated footprint pixels are emitted as debris particles that accumulate in the shared store -> expect a substantial, growing particle count. Observed: exactly 63 debris particles shed by tick 16 (up to 8/tick capped, deterministic across repeated runs), staying at 63 for the remainder of the run; the >= 20.0 floor is a loose pin, the accumulation is the a-priori prediction. The CPM->particle mass ledger closes: 63 shed particles == 63 distinct vacated pixels (no double-count) <= 69 unique vacated pixels; the 63-vs-56px gap is legitimate footprint drift, not manufactured mass (tests/test_disintegration_ledger.py::test_cpm_particle_ledger_closes_and_double_count_is_fixed, tests/test_disintegration_regime.py::test_cell_holds_then_disintegrates_into_scattering_debris)

behavior_tests.name: cpm-particle-mass-ledger-closes
behavior_tests.description: The CPM->particle conversion conserves mass -- every shed debris particle is a distinct vacated lattice pixel, so the shed count equals the distinct-vacated-pixel count and never exceeds the total unique vacated pixels. Answers peer-review issue M5 (the apparent 68-vs-56 double-count).

measure.expr: n_particles_shed vs distinct-vacated-pixels vs unique-vacated-pixels over the release phase

pass_if.provenance: built an external CPM->particle mass ledger (never reading the process's private state or the movement-scrambled particle positions) that replays the footprint diff vacated = prev_fp & ~curr_fp tick by tick. Measured on the fixed-seed run: 75 per-tick vacation events over 69 unique pixels; the pre-fix policy min(vacated, cap) shed 68 particles over only 62 distinct pixels -- 6 re-vacated pixels double-shed (6 units of manufactured mass, exactly the M5 68-vs-56 gap). An already-shed-pixel guard now sheds 63 particles at 63 distinct pixels, equal to the live particle-store growth and <= 69 unique vacated; the ledger closes -- shed material, not deleted-then-recreated mass (tests/test_disintegration_ledger.py::test_cpm_particle_ledger_closes_and_double_count_is_fixed, tests/test_disintegration_mass.py::test_shed_particles_equal_fresh_vacated_pixels_within_per_tick_cap)

behavior_tests.name: debris-cloud-keeps-scattering
behavior_tests.description: The debris cloud's RMS spread strictly increases after dissolution completes -- genuine scattering under BrownianMovement, not particles piling up or stalling.

measure.expr: RMS radius of particle positions, tick 22 vs tick 16

pass_if.provenance: prior: once the domain has dissolved, its shed debris drifts under Brownian scatter, so the cloud's RMS spread strictly increases (does not stall or pile against a wall). Observed: RMS spread grows monotonically over an 8-tick post-dissolution window from ~5.3 (tick 16, dissolution complete) to ~7.6 (tick 24). BrownianMovement is unseeded, so the exact magnitudes vary run-to-run (representative values shown); the strict INCREASE is the a-priori prediction and the robust, test-asserted claim (tests/test_disintegration_regime.py::test_cell_holds_then_disintegrates_into_scattering_debris)

behavior_tests.name: particle-bridge-emits-then-scatters
behavior_tests.description: Foundational control (not this study's scientific claim): the CPM-to-particle bridge this study depends on -- a process emitting particles via the map `_add` sentinel, moved by a separate stock BrownianMovement process -- works correctly, independent of any disintegration mechanism.

measure.expr: len(particles) unchanged and >=2 positions moved, tick 1 vs tick 4

pass_if.provenance: a synthetic emitter process (not this study's composite): 3 particles emitted on tick 1, still exactly 3 particles at tick 4, with at least 2 having moved -- an exact integer-count pin, exact only while the emitter and engine are fixed (tests/test_particle_bridge_spike.py::test_emit_then_scatter)

findings.statement:
A single real CPM cell coupled to a real spatio-flux acetate field through one
coupling process (`CpmDisintegration`) reproduces the paper's §Disintegration level-shift
(Fig 6) as spatial dissolution with a scripted resorption schedule (resorb_per_tick=6.0) --
simulation-derived trigger timing, scripted resorption ramp: the cell holds coherent while the
diffusing acetate field is below its
footprint-local viability bound, then latches a release once that bound is crossed at a
specific, deterministic tick, and its domain resorbs to full dissolution over the following
ticks. Confirmed: area > 30 through tick 6, released_tick == 7.0, area == 0 by tick 16, all
deterministic across repeated runs.

The cell's vacated footprint pixels appear as physical debris rather than vanishing.
As the domain resorbs, its vacated footprint pixels are emitted as particles in a shared
map[particle] store, and that debris cloud keeps scattering (RMS spread strictly increasing)
well after the cell itself has fully dissolved, under a separate stock BrownianMovement
process. Confirmed: 63 particles shed by tick 16 (deterministic, reproduces exactly); RMS
spread ~5.3 -> ~7.6 over an 8-tick post-dissolution window in a representative run --
BrownianMovement is unseeded, so the exact magnitudes vary run-to-run, but the strict increase
is the robust, test-asserted claim. Mass IS conserved through the transition -- shed material,
not deleted-then-recreated mass: a CPM->particle ledger closes it (each shed particle is a
distinct vacated lattice pixel, so 63 shed == 63 distinct vacated pixels <= 69 unique vacated).
The 63-vs-56px gap is legitimate footprint drift -- the cell traverses 69 distinct pixels over
its released lifetime as its shape reshapes while resorbing, not the 56 held at the release
instant. Building the ledger caught and fixed a real double-count (a pre-fix logic shed 68
particles over only 62 distinct pixels, re-shedding 6 re-vacated pixels); the fixed shedding
guards against re-shedding any pixel.

evidence.observed: 63 particles shed == 63 distinct vacated pixels <= 69 unique vacated (ledger closes, pre-fix double-count of 6 found and fixed); RMS spread ~5.3 (tick 16) -> ~7.6 (tick 24) (representative -- BrownianMovement is unseeded, exact magnitudes vary run-to-run)

findings.statement:
The CPM-to-particle bridge this study's disintegration mechanism depends on --
that a process can emit particles via the map `_add` sentinel into a shared map[particle]
store, and a separate stock movement process can then move them -- is runtime-verified
directly and independently of the disintegration mechanism itself, retiring what was
previously an untested primitive. Confirmed structurally: a synthetic emitter's 3 particles
remain exactly 3 particles four ticks later, with at least 2 having moved under
BrownianMovement.

evidence.observed: 3 particles emitted, unchanged count 4 ticks later, >=2 moved

regression_compatibility.basis:
disintegration-spatial.composite.json builds and runs to completion through the
process-bigraph engine (tests/test_cpm_disintegration.py, tests/test_disintegration_regime.py,
tests/test_disintegration_viz.py, tests/test_particle_bridge_spike.py); guarded skip when
the optional cpm/spatio_flux dependencies are absent, matching this investigation's
flagship and companion studies' convention.

biological_validation.basis: All primary behavior tests pass on measured readouts from a real 20-24 tick run -- the cell holds coherent, crosses its viability bound at a specific tick, resorbs to full dissolution, and sheds debris that keeps scattering after dissolution completes. The CPM trajectory (hold/cross/resorb, released_tick, area, shed particle count) is fixed-seed deterministic and reproduces exactly; the debris scatter's RMS-spread magnitude moves under unseeded BrownianMovement, so its exact values are representative of one run, not run-to-run-reproducible -- only the strict-increase direction is asserted as the robust claim. The foundational particle-bridge control also passes, independent of the disintegration mechanism.

explanatory_gain.basis:
Realizing the paper's §Disintegration level-shift (Fig 6) with a real CPM cell's structural viability collapsing
under a real diffusing acetate field -- rather than a scripted viability scalar decaying
on a timer -- makes this investigation's disintegration claim (a cellular description
stops being adequate and the right level of description drops to interacting molecular
components) concrete at real spatial, per-pixel resolution: the shed "molecular components"
are literal scattering particles in a shared field, not an abstract debris variable.

conclusion:
## Claims
- Composing one real CPM cell with a real spatio-flux acetate field and a real spatio-flux particle-movement process through two coupling processes (`CpmDisintegration` for the viability-collapse trigger and resorption, stock `BrownianMovement` for the debris scatter) reproduces the paper's §Disintegration level-shift (Fig 6) as spatial dissolution with a scripted resorption ramp (resorb_per_tick=6.0) -- simulation-derived trigger timing, scripted resorption. Over a 20-24 tick run: the cell holds coherent (area > 30) through tick 6, the footprint-local acetate mean crosses viability_threshold at released_tick == 7, the domain resorbs to area 0 by tick 16, and sheds 63 particles -- the CPM trajectory (hold/cross/resorb, released_tick, area, shed particle count) is fixed-seed deterministic and reproduces exactly. The CPM->particle mass ledger closes -- 63 shed == 63 distinct vacated pixels <= 69 unique vacated, shed material not deleted-then-recreated mass (building it caught and fixed a real 6-pixel double-count; see limitations). The debris cloud's RMS spread keeps strictly increasing through tick 24 (~5.3 -> ~7.6 in a representative run); BrownianMovement is unseeded, so those exact magnitudes vary run-to-run -- only the strict increase is the robust, reproducible claim.
- The stressor is literally `acetate` -- the SAME molecule that is metabolic waste and cross-feeding food in `cell-cell-coupling`, here a toxin whose high local concentration crosses the cell's viability bound. This carries the paper's closing relational-molecule claim (§Cell–cell coupling): one molecule counting as nutrient, signal, or toxin through its consequences for viability -- nutrient/food there, toxin here.
- The two phases realize §Disintegration's failure cascade end to end: an actively maintained, far-from-equilibrium CPM domain, once viability is lost, relaxes into a diffusion-dominated, equilibrating debris cloud under `BrownianMovement`. Most models skip this transition explicitly -- agent-based models remove cells mid-simulation and whole-cell models assume viability -- so carrying a coherent domain through its own dissolution into diffusing debris is the explanatory gain.

## Evidence
- **CELL-HOLDS-COHERENT-BEFORE-CROSSING** -- area 61-66 through tick 6, released False, 0 particles
- **STRESSOR-CROSSES-VIABILITY-BOUND** -- released_tick == 7.0, deterministic
- **DOMAIN-RESORBS-TO-ZERO** -- area falls from 56 (tick 7) to 0 (tick 16)
- **SHED-MATERIAL-BECOMES-DEBRIS-PARTICLES** -- 63 debris particles by tick 16, each a distinct vacated pixel
- **CPM-PARTICLE-MASS-LEDGER-CLOSES** -- 63 shed == 63 distinct vacated pixels <= 69 unique vacated; a pre-fix double-count of 6 re-vacated pixels found and fixed (answers peer-review M5)
- **DEBRIS-CLOUD-KEEPS-SCATTERING** -- RMS spread ~5.3 (tick 16) -> ~7.6 (tick 24), a representative run (BrownianMovement is unseeded; the strict increase is the robust claim)
- **PARTICLE-BRIDGE-EMITS-THEN-SCATTERS** -- 3 synthetic particles emitted then scattered, bridge verified independently

## Limitations
- The disintegration mechanism realized here is resorption + particle-shedding, not in-lattice fragmentation -- the connectivity/E1 structural-integrity constraint is a verified no-op in this viva-cpm build, and lambda_volume/temperature are init-only with no runtime setters, so a settled domain cannot be shattered into scattered pixels in-lattice. This is a chosen realization of "the coherent domain dissolves," not emergent lattice fragmentation -- a real engine limitation, documented in the API map.
- Debris particles move under spatio-flux BrownianMovement (NumPy diffusion), not rigid-body pymunk physics -- they drift and scatter, they do not collide or fall.
- The acetate gradient, viability_threshold, resorb_per_tick, max_particles_per_tick, and diffusion coefficients are toy-real -- plausible, hand-tuned magnitudes chosen to make the full arc legible within a 20-24 tick run, not fitted to a named stressor or material.
- Unlike studies 2-3 in this investigation, this study's CPM cell has no metabolism/cobra path at all -- CpmDisintegration is built around the viability-collapse trigger alone.
- The released flag latches permanently once crossed and never un-crosses, even once the footprint empties and would otherwise read a misleadingly low stressor mean.

## Next steps
- Extend the debris-scatter mechanism with pymunk rigid-body physics so shed particles can collide and settle, rather than only diffusing.
- Investigate whether the connectivity/E1 no-op is a genuine viva-cpm upstream bug worth reporting, since a working structural-integrity lock would let a future study demonstrate in-lattice fragmentation directly.
- Fan out to the next spatial counterpart in the planned increments.

disintegration-spatial.composite.json builds and runs to completion

if_primary_tests_pass.biological_validation: The spatial §Disintegration level-shift pattern (Fig 6) is demonstrated at the toy-real (uncalibrated) level, with genuine per-pixel CPM shape dynamics, a real diffusing acetate field, and a verified particle bridge behind the hold-cross-resorb-scatter arc, rather than a scripted trajectory.

diagnose: the cell fails to hold coherent before crossing (the acetate gradient is too aggressive, or the cell's viability threshold is being crossed spuriously at the seed footprint)
released_tick drifts or the released flag never latches (the diffusion coefficient or gradient shape no longer brings the footprint-local mean above threshold within the run)
the domain fails to resorb to 0 (resorb_per_tick too small relative to the run length, or the target-volume ramp is not being applied after release)
shed particles are missing or the debris cloud stops scattering (the CPM-to-particle bridge is broken, or BrownianMovement is not wired to the particles store)
if_primary_tests_fail.block_downstream: any future spatial study reusing the CpmDisintegration pattern or the CPM-to-particle bridge (e.g. a spatial growth-and-division study that needs to shed material on division)

A settled CPM domain cannot be shattered into scattered pixels in-lattice in this build -- the code-verified route is to resorb the cell and convert its shed pixels into particles. This is framed as a chosen, honest realization of "the coherent domain dissolves," not as emergent lattice fragmentation -- a real, documented engine limitation.

Debris particles move under spatio-flux BrownianMovement (NumPy diffusion), not rigid-body pymunk physics -- the particles drift and scatter, they do not collide with each other or with the dissolving cell, and do not fall under gravity.

The acetate field's radial gradient, viability_threshold, resorb_per_tick, max_particles_per_tick, and the diffusion coefficients (acetate D=4.0, debris diffusion_rate=1.0) are toy-real, hand-tuned magnitudes chosen to make hold-cross-resorb-scatter all legible within a 20-24 tick run -- not fitted to a named stressor, material, or literature target.

Unlike studies 2-3 in this investigation (cell-environment-coupling, cell-cell-coupling), this study's CPM cell has no metabolism/cobra path at all -- CpmDisintegration is deliberately built around the viability-collapse trigger alone, not nutrient uptake or growth.

The released flag latches once the crossing happens and never un-crosses, even once the footprint empties and its mean-stressor reading would otherwise read misleadingly low -- a deliberate design choice so a dissolved cell cannot spuriously "recover" viability.

The CPM-to-particle bridge (a process emitting particles via the map `_add` sentinel into a shared map[particle] store, moved by a separate stock BrownianMovement process) is now runtime-verified directly (tests/test_particle_bridge_spike.py), independent of the disintegration mechanism itself -- previously an unverified primitive.

The CPM->particle mass ledger is CLOSED (answers peer-review issue M5, previously PENDING). An external ledger -- reading only the CPM lattice via world.snapshot(), never the process's private state nor the movement-scrambled particle positions -- replays the footprint diff vacated = prev_fp & ~curr_fp tick by tick. Building it caught a REAL double-count: the pre-fix shedding (min(vacated, cap), no memory) shed 68 particles over only 62 distinct pixels, because a pixel can be vacated, re-occupied by ordinary CPM fluctuation as the footprint drifts while resorbing, then vacated again -- and was shed a second time at the same pixel center (6 such re-vacated pixels = 6 units of manufactured mass, exactly the 68-vs-56 gap M5 flagged). Note the weak bound shed(68) <= unique_vacated(69) held even for the buggy version, which is why it masked the bug -- only shed == distinct-pixels exposes it. Fixed with an already-shed-pixel guard (cap now counts FRESH emissions): the process sheds 63 particles at 63 distinct pixels, equal to the live particle-store growth and <= 69 unique vacated pixels. The ledger closes -- shed material, not deleted-then-recreated mass. The 63-vs-56px gap is legitimate footprint drift: the cell traverses 69 distinct lattice pixels over its released lifetime, not the 56 held at the release instant. The remaining 69-63 = 6 gap is the per-tick cap dropping the steepest vacation ticks (vacated-but-unshed, the safe under-counting direction), never mass double-counted (tests/test_disintegration_ledger.py, tests/test_disintegration_mass.py).

Read against a lumped, specification-stage realization of the same pattern: that
kind of model closes the paper's §Disintegration level-shift (Fig 6) with a scripted viability scalar
decaying on a thermal-shock
timer, over a lumped cell-state composite. This study closes the same level-shift with a real
CPM cell's structural viability collapsing under a real diffusing acetate field, its domain
genuinely resorbing in lattice pixels rather than a scalar dropping toward zero, and its shed
material becoming literal scattering particles rather than an abstract debris variable. Compare
the two for the same disintegration claim at two very different mechanistic resolutions.
falsifiability: Overturned if the cell fails to hold coherent before the acetate crosses its viability bound, if the crossing tick is not deterministic across repeated runs of the same composite, if the domain fails to resorb to near-zero area within the run, if shed pixels do not appear as particles in the shared store, if the debris cloud's RMS spread fails to increase after dissolution completes (implying stalling or wall-saturation rather than genuine scattering), or if the foundational CPM-to-particle bridge control fails to preserve particle count or produce movement.

experiment: Run the `disintegration-spatial` composite (`CpmDisintegration`, a single CPM cell on a shared 60x60 field grid inside a radial acetate gradient, coupled to a stock `BrownianMovement` particle-scatter process) to completion over 20-24 ticks through the process-bigraph engine, and measure whether a diffusing acetate field crossing a CPM cell's own viability bound is enough to trigger structural dissolution (domain resorption) and convert its shed material into a genuinely scattering debris cloud.
result: Over a 20-24 tick run, the CPM cell holds coherent (area > 30) through tick 6, the footprint-local acetate mean crosses viability_threshold at released_tick == 7, the domain resorbs to area 0 by tick 16, and sheds exactly 63 particles into a shared debris store -- the CPM trajectory (hold/cross/resorb, released_tick, area, shed particle count) is fixed-seed deterministic and reproduces exactly run to run. The CPM->particle mass ledger closes (63 shed == 63 distinct vacated pixels <= 69 unique vacated -- shed material, not deleted-then-recreated mass; building it caught and fixed a real 6-pixel double-count). That debris cloud's RMS spread keeps strictly increasing through tick 24 (~5.3 -> ~7.6 in a representative run) -- genuine scattering, not wall-saturation; BrownianMovement is unseeded, so the exact RMS magnitudes vary run-to-run and are representative rather than reproducible, but the strict increase is the robust, test-asserted claim. The paper's §Disintegration level-shift (Fig 6) holds as spatial dissolution with a scripted resorption ramp (resorb_per_tick=6.0) -- the trigger timing is simulation-derived, the resorption schedule is scripted -- composed from independent frameworks (viva-cpm + spatio-flux particles) through one coupling process plus one stock movement process. The stressor here is literally `acetate`, the SAME molecule that is metabolic waste and cross-feeding food in `cell-cell-coupling` -- one molecule whose meaning is set relationally by each cell's interface (§Cell–cell coupling): nutrient there, toxin here. And the scatter phase reads directly as §Disintegration's failure cascade -- the actively maintained, far-from-equilibrium cell relaxing, once viability is lost, into a diffusion-dominated debris cloud, the transition most models skip (agent-based models delete the cell, whole-cell models assume viability).

The CPM trajectory (hold/cross/resorb, released_tick, area, shed particle count) is fixed-seed deterministic and reproduces exactly; the debris scatter's RMS-spread magnitude moves under unseeded BrownianMovement, so its exact values are representative of one run, not run-to-run-reproducible -- only the strict-increase direction is asserted as the robust claim. under a real diffusing acetate field -- rather than a scripted viability scalar decaying
on a timer -- makes this investigation's disintegration claim (a cellular description
stops being adequate and the right level of description drops to interacting molecular

A single real CPM cell coupled to a real spatio-flux acetate field through one
coupling process (`CpmDisintegration`) reproduces the paper's §Disintegration level-shift
(Fig 6) as spatial dissolution with a scripted resorption schedule (resorb_per_tick=6.0) --
simulation-derived trigger timing, scripted resorption ramp: the cell holds coherent while the
diffusing acetate field is below its
footprint-local viability bound, then latches a release once that bound is crossed at a
specific, deterministic tick, and its domain resorbs to full dissolution over the following
ticks. Confirmed: area > 30 through tick 6, released_tick == 7.0, area == 0 by tick 16, all
deterministic across repeated runs.
